archetype.name: Lost Season (April hole)
archetype.definition: A 74-88 year in which a 7-19 April dug a hole the Mets never escaped, and a thin lineup and a broken bullpen kept a good rotation from mattering.

report.headline: A 7-19 April buried a team that roughly broke even after it

recap.finish: 74-88, fifth in the NL East, 20 games behind Atlanta; missed the postseason
recap.body:
This was a mediocre team that had one catastrophic month, and that month decided the year. The Mets were outscored 731-699 overall, a -0.2 Run Diff / G that ranked 19th, with the offense 21st and run prevention 18th. Neither side was terrible on its own. Neither was good enough to carry the other, and the record finished below what even that modest deficit implied.

The season turned in April. After a 3-2 March, the Mets went 7-19 and were outscored 123-84. The 12-game losing streak, the longest of the year, set against a longest winning streak of just four, shows a team that could sink fast but never surged. From May on they went 64-67 and scored 593 runs while allowing 590. That is a .500 team, and a .500 team can't dig out of a 12-games-under start. May (16-12) and August (15-12) were the only clearly winning months, and June's 10-17 undid most of May.

The rotation earned its B. Nolan McLean was the staff's anchor: a 3.16 ERA, 194 strikeouts and 3.5 WAR over almost 180 innings. Christian Scott's 3.61 FIP backed up a 3.85 ERA. Sean Manaea's 4.78 ERA over 150.2 innings was the soft spot. The bullpen, graded D, gave back what the starters built. Kodai Senga threw the most relief innings (61.1) with a 7.34 ERA and a 14.5% walk rate, and Tobias Myers posted a 5.53. A -3.7 W vs Run Diff, 24th in the league, fits a pen that lost close games, and this is the third time in four years the Mets have finished on the wrong side of that number.

The lineup was the bigger structural problem. Team OPS fell to .706 (23rd) from .753 a year earlier. Juan Soto was the lone true force with a 147 wRC+ and 27 homers, but he played only 111 games. Carson Benge was the most valuable Met at 4.3 WAR, pairing a 118 wRC+ with 22 steals and 9.6 Def Runs. Around them sat a lot of league-average-or-worse volume. Bo Bichette led the team in plate appearances (696) with a 96 wRC+. Francisco Lindor hit .225 in 105 games. Marcus Semien gave 547 plate appearances of 74 wRC+ hitting and -7.9 Def Runs for -0.5 WAR, which nearly accounts for the team's below-average Fielding Runs by himself.

The ending was quiet: a 5-5 final ten, including a split with Philadelphia, with the season long decided. The bigger story is the trend. The run differential has gone from +0.44 per game in 2024 to +0.31 in 2025 to -0.2 now, and the offense rank slid from 7th to 10th to 21st over the same span.

highlights.title: McLean anchors a real rotation
highlights.body: Nolan McLean pitched like a front-line starter, with a 3.16 ERA and 26% strikeout rate over nearly 180 innings, and a 3.59 FIP says most of it was earned. Christian Scott's 3.61 FIP adds a second strong arm, and the group graded B even with Manaea's struggles. This is the part of the roster most likely to hold up.

highlights.title: Benge's all-around breakout value
highlights.body: Carson Benge led the team with 4.3 WAR by doing everything: a 118 wRC+, 22 steals and 9.6 Def Runs over 156 games. His value doesn't rest on one hot skill, so it should be durable. He and Soto were the only clearly above-average bats in the everyday group.

highlights.title: Soto still elite when available
highlights.body: Juan Soto's 147 wRC+ and .393 OBP made him the lineup's engine and an All-Star. The catch is 111 games. The lineup had no one close to replacing that production when he sat.

lowlights.title: April sank the season early
lowlights.body: A 7-19 April with a 39-run deficit put the Mets 12 games under .500 before May. They were essentially even the rest of the way, outscoring opponents by 3 runs, but with a longest winning streak of four they never strung together a run to recover.

lowlights.title: Bullpen gave away the margins
lowlights.body: The pen graded D, and its highest-innings arm, Senga, posted a 7.34 ERA with a 14.5% walk rate. A -3.7 W vs Run Diff points to close games lost late. Devin Williams' 3.05 FIP against a 4.43 ERA suggests the closer was partly unlucky, but the depth behind him was simply poor.

lowlights.title: Lineup thinned out badly
lowlights.body: Team OPS fell from .753 to .706 in a year, and several heavy-usage spots hit below average. Semien's 74 wRC+ and -7.9 Def Runs in 547 PA were the worst of it, and Bichette's 96 wRC+ in a team-high 696 PA added little. That is a roster-construction problem, not bad luck.

arc.note: A disastrous 7-19 April was followed by alternating months: a strong May, a bad June and July, and a mildly winning August and an even September. It added up to roughly .500 ball that couldn't erase the opening hole.

recap.nextYear: The foundation is in the rotation and two outfielders. McLean and Scott pitched like legitimate starters with FIPs to match, and Benge and Soto produced most of the lineup's value. Some numbers will move on their own. Zac Thornton's 3.42 ERA sits on a 4.51 FIP and should rise, while Williams' 3.05 FIP says his ERA should fall. The -3.7 W vs Run Diff is mostly luck, but even an even break only lifts this team to about 78 wins, because the run differential itself was negative. The real work is the bullpen behind Williams and a lineup whose offense rank has fallen from 7th to 21st in two years, starting with second base and the volume of near-average plate appearances around Soto and Benge.

confidence.note: Full 162-game season; the April collapse and the bullpen and lineup weaknesses are large and consistent signals.
